blocks.text: **Binary search** finds a value in a **sorted** array by repeatedly checking the middle of the part still in play. Because the array is sorted, one comparison with the middle value tells you which half the target must be in — so the other half is thrown away without looking at it. Halving again and again, a billion values shrink to one in about 30 steps.

blocks.alt: Searching 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91 for 23. Step 1: low is index 0, high is 9, mid is 4 holding 16; 16 is smaller than 23, so the target is to the right and low becomes 5. Step 2: mid is 7 holding 56, bigger than 23, so high becomes 6. Step 3: mid is 5 holding 23 — found.

items: Keep two indexes around the part still in play: `low = 0` and `high = n - 1`.
While `low <= high`, look at the middle index `mid`.
If `nums[mid]` is **smaller** than the target, the target can only be to its right: `low = mid + 1`.
If it's **bigger**, the target can only be to its left: `high = mid - 1`.
If the loop ends (`low > high`), nothing is left in play: the target isn't there. Return -1.

blocks.caption: Watch the search space shrink by half at every step, until the target is found or nothing is left.

blocks.text: Each step at least halves the search space: n, n/2, n/4, … down to 1. The number of halvings from n to 1 is **log₂ n**. So binary search does at most about log₂ n + 1 checks, and uses **O(1)** extra space.

blocks.code:
n = 16             ->  at most 5 checks
n = 1,000          ->  at most 10
n = 1,000,000      ->  at most 20
n = 1,000,000,000  ->  at most 30

blocks.alt: Linear search: O(n) time, O(1) space. Binary search: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: Binary search is short but famous for off-by-one bugs. The cure is to know exactly what `low` and `high` mean and keep it true every step. Here the rule is: **if the target is in the array, it's somewhere in `nums[low..high]`, both ends included.**

items: It starts true: `low = 0`, `high = n - 1` cover everything.

`low = mid + 1` and `high = mid - 1` keep it true: `mid` was just checked and isn't the target, so it can be dropped. Dropping it also guarantees **progress** — the range always shrinks, so the loop can't run forever.
The loop runs while the range is non-empty, `low <= high`. A one-value range (`low == high`) still gets checked.
When `low > high` the range is empty — the invariant says the target isn't there.

blocks.text: **The safe midpoint.** `(low + high) / 2` overflows a 32-bit int when both are near 2³¹ — a bug that sat in Java's own library for nine years. `low + (high - low) / 2` gives the same middle without overflowing. (Python's integers can't overflow, and JavaScript's numbers are exact far beyond any array length.)
The same idea as a function that calls itself on the half that's left. It reads closer to the definition, but uses **O(log n)** stack space, so the loop is usually preferred.

items: **`while (low < high)` with `high = mid - 1`** — the last one-value range is never checked, so a target sitting there is missed.
**`low = mid` or `high = mid` in this template** — when the range is two values, mid can equal low, nothing changes, and the loop never ends.
**Searching unsorted data** — binary search silently returns wrong answers.
**Duplicates** — this version returns *some* index of the target, not necessarily the first. For the first or last, use the lower and upper bound templates (next lesson).
Check the middle; throw away the half that can't hold the target; repeat.
**O(log n)** time, **O(1)** space — 30 checks for a billion values.
Invariant: the target, if present, is in `nums[low..high]`; loop while `low <= high`; move to `mid ± 1`.
Use `low + (high - low) / 2` in Java and C++.
